name: Lymphomatoid papulosis
aliases: CD30-positive lymphoproliferative disorder of the skin

clinicalPearls: Presents as recurrent crops of self-regressing papules and nodules that may ulcerate and heal spontaneously over weeks, often leaving scars
Belongs to the spectrum of primary cutaneous CD30-positive lymphoproliferative disorders and follows a chronic but indolent course despite atypical, alarming histology
Multiple histological subtypes (including types A, B, C, D, and E) exist and can coexist, sometimes closely mimicking mycosis fungoides or anaplastic large-cell lymphoma microscopically
The atypical cells are usually CD30-positive T-cells, and clonal T-cell receptor rearrangements are common yet do not equate to systemic malignancy
There is an increased lifetime risk of an associated lymphoma, particularly mycosis fungoides, primary cutaneous anaplastic large-cell lymphoma, or Hodgkin lymphoma
The clinicopathological correlation is essential: the benign, waxing-and-waning clinical behaviour distinguishes it from aggressive lymphoma
Management is often expectant, with skin-directed therapy or low-dose methotrexate for extensive or symptomatic disease
reference.pathophysiology: Lymphomatoid papulosis is an indolent, chronic clonal proliferation of CD30-positive T-lymphocytes confined to the skin. Despite harbouring monoclonal T-cell receptor rearrangements and cytologically atypical, often anaplastic-looking cells, the lesions characteristically regress spontaneously, reflecting effective local immune control and apoptosis of the neoplastic clone. The same aberrant clone can, in a minority of patients, underlie or precede an associated lymphoma such as mycosis fungoides, cutaneous anaplastic large-cell lymphoma, or Hodgkin lymphoma, placing lymphomatoid papulosis at the indolent end of the CD30-positive lymphoproliferative spectrum.
additionalDifferentials: Arthropod bite reactions or other benign papular eruptions
Systemic anaplastic large-cell lymphoma with skin involvement
Cutaneous involvement by other T-cell lymphomas
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy with immunohistochemistry for CD30 and T-cell markers
T-cell receptor clonality analysis of lesional skin
Clinicopathological correlation documenting the self-regressing behaviour
Surveillance for an associated systemic or cutaneous lymphoma
Staging investigations only if a concurrent lymphoma is suspected clinically
Photographic mapping to monitor the recurrent, migratory eruption
redFlags: A lesion that fails to regress and progressively enlarges, suggesting cutaneous anaplastic large-cell lymphoma
New lymphadenopathy or systemic symptoms indicating an associated lymphoma
Development of persistent plaques or tumours typical of mycosis fungoides
Rapidly evolving widespread disease that departs from the usual indolent pattern
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent with a normal life expectancy in most patients, but lifelong surveillance is warranted because a subset develop an associated lymphoma over time.
pitfalls: Overtreating a benign, self-regressing condition as aggressive lymphoma because of alarming histology
Interpreting a clonal T-cell population as proof of systemic malignancy
Missing an evolving associated lymphoma through inadequate follow-up
Confusing type C histology with primary cutaneous anaplastic large-cell lymphoma without clinical correlation
references: Swerdlow SH et al. WHO monograph on lymphoid neoplasms
